newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran names four to run in presidential election.
newsitem.headline: Iran names four to run in presidential election.

text.p: A powerful Islamic screening body on Wednesday passed judgment on more than 200 Iranians vying for President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani's job, rejecting all but four as candidates to stand in the country's May 23 election.

The Guardian Council, a body of six clerics and six lawyers responsible for screening election candidates, said in a statement reported by Iran's official news agency IRNA only four presidential hopefuls out of 238 had passed scrutiny.

It named them as Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, who is speaker of the Majlis (parliament), Mohammad Mohammadi Reyshahri, a former intelligence minister, Mohammad Khatami, a former minister of culture and Islamic guidance, and Reza Zavarei, deputy head of the judiciary. All four are Shi'ite Moslems and only Zavarei is not a clergyman.
The council screened the contenders for their allegiance to Iran's religious leadership and Islamic system of government.

The rejected candidates included nine women, one of them the daughter of one of the ayatollahs who led the 1979 Islamic revolution that toppled the Shah. The nine had sought a legal ruling on women's right to run for president for the first time.
Campaigning is due to start on Saturday for the election in which Nateq-Nouri and Khatami appear to be front-runners.
Nateq-Nouri, who is close to Iran's traditional bazaar merchants, is backed by key clerical groups and by the majority conservative faction in the Majlis.
Khatami draws support from a coalition of pro-Rafsanjani centrists and Islamist left-wingers who have moderated many of their views in recent years.

A public opinion poll published in the daily Tehran Times on Wednesday gave 40.8 percent of popular support to Nateq-Nouri, 33.8 percent to Khatami and 8.2 percent to Reyshahri. The remaining 17.2 percent chose other candidates, were undecided or did not respond. It surveyed 1,182 Tehran residents in April.

Tehran residents said Khatami appeared to be gaining wide support among women, young people and intellectuals who fear a harder application of Islamic rules governing everyday life and restrictions on freedom of expression if Nateq-Nouri is elected.

But Iranian analysts said recent remarks by Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei were likely to provide ammunition for Nateq-Nouri's backers who question Khatami's whole-hearted allegience to Islamic principles.

"The (Iranian) nation will certainly not vote for any candidate who shows the least flexibility towards America, towards the Western states' interference, and towards foreign political and cultural aggression," Khamenei said on Wednesday in a speech carried by Tehran radio.
Khamenei on Saturday told a gathering of clergymen they should help voters make the right choice by telling them who the best candidate was according to Islamic principles.

The analysts said the call was likely to boost Nateq-Nouri's chances by prompting mainstream clerics to launch a publicity campaign in his support during majour annual Shi'ite mourning ceremonies a week before the election.

Rafsanjani must stand down in August after two four-year terms as president but is expected to continue to wield considerable influence in state affairs as head of a powerful body that will draw up government policies and advise Khamenei.
Since his election by a landslide in 1989, Rafsanjani has tried to reconcile Iran's revolutionary ideals with the task of solving daunting economic problems aggravated by U.S. sanctions.
Despite the problems, the International Monetary Fund recently expressed satisfaction with Iran's economic policy and praised it for reviving growth and curbing inflation.
